When you want to compare means across more than two groups, a t-test isn't enough — that's where ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) comes in.

ANOVA checks if there is any significant difference in means across the groups. It doesn't tell you which groups differ — just whether at least one group is different. You can follow up with post-hoc tests if needed.

In our example, if we want to look at differences in self-care across more than two areas, we can use an ANOVA. We can also treat this as a linear regression, but we will go over that later.

In order to find the relationship between two variables without attempting to predict one from the other, we can do a Pearson's correlation. Pearson's correlation is the default, but you can change it to be a Spearman's or other kind of correlation if you need it.

Lastly, as an example for logistic regression, we can look at whether people were more likely to submit a grant if they spent less time on TikTok and ingested more caffeine. 
```{r}
log_model<-glm(submitted_grant~tiktok_min_S2 + caffeine_mg_S2, data=GradLife,family="binomial")

summary(log_model)
```
